title: Unit 6: Predictive Distributions
text: Based on the corresponding unit in the supplied STAT 251 Midterm Exam Topics guide. Numerical examples are illustrative, not additional course data.

title: Unit 6: Predictive Distributions
text:
Parameters versus future observations
The posterior \(\pi(\theta\mid y_{\rm obs})\) describes an unknown parameter. The posterior predictive distribution describes new data, combining parameter uncertainty with sampling variation. Assume new data are conditionally independent of the observed data given \(\theta\): \[f(y_{\rm new}\mid y_{\rm obs})=\int f(y_{\rm new}\mid\theta)\pi(\theta\mid y_{\rm obs})\,d\theta.\] Use a sum for a discrete parameter. A credible interval for \(\theta\) and a predictive interval for a future count refer to different objects and scales.

title: Unit 6: Predictive Distributions
text:
Monte Carlo prediction
Draw \(\theta^{(j)}\) from the posterior, then draw \(Y_{\rm new}^{(j)}\) from the sampling distribution conditional on that draw. For a batch of \(m\) future Bernoulli trials, draw one shared parameter per batch and then a binomial count.

set.seed(253)
A <- 9; B <- 5; m <- 20; J <- 50000
theta <- rbeta(J, A, B)
y_new <- rbinom(J, size = m, prob = theta)
c(mean_count = mean(y_new), prob_at_least_15 = mean(y_new >= 15))

      mean_count prob_at_least_15 
        12.86274          0.32890 

quantile(y_new, c(0.025, 0.975))

 2.5% 97.5% 
    6    19 

# Alternative: average conditional probabilities (less simulation noise).
mean(pbinom(14, m, theta, lower.tail = FALSE))

[1] 0.3294873


The integer quantile interval can contain more than 95% probability because discrete counts do not allow arbitrary tail probabilities.

title: Unit 6: Predictive Distributions
section: Derive the exact beta-binomial predictive distribution
text:
Derive the exact beta-binomial predictive distribution
Suppose \(\theta\mid y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(A,B)\) and \(K\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\theta)\). For \(k=0,\ldots,m\), \[\begin{aligned}
P(K=k\mid y)
&=\int_0^1\binom mk\theta^k(1-\theta)^{m-k}
\frac{\theta^{A-1}(1-\theta)^{B-1}}{B(A,B)}\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{\binom mk}{B(A,B)}\int_0^1\theta^{A+k-1}(1-\theta)^{B+m-k-1}\,d\theta\\
&=\binom mk\frac{B(A+k,B+m-k)}{B(A,B)}.
\end{aligned}\] The probability is zero outside the integer support. This is \(\operatorname{BetaBinomial}(m,A,B)\), with \[E(K\mid y)=m\mu,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(K\mid y)=m\mu(1-\mu)\frac{A+B+m}{A+B+1},\quad \mu=\frac A{A+B}.\]

k <- 0:m
exact <- exp(lchoose(m, k) + lbeta(A+k, B+m-k) - lbeta(A, B))
stopifnot(abs(sum(exact)-1) < 1e-10)
simulated <- tabulate(y_new+1, nbins = m+1)/J
matplot(k, cbind(exact, simulated), type = "b", pch = c(16,1),
        col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"), lty = c(1,2),
        xlab = "Future successes", ylab = "Probability")
legend("topleft", c("Exact", "Monte Carlo"), col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"),
       lty = c(1,2), pch = c(16,1), bty = "n")







sum(exact[k >= 15])

[1] 0.3293289


Log beta functions and log binomial coefficients avoid direct evaluation of very large factorials or tiny products.

title: Unit 6: Predictive Distributions
text:
Plug-in prediction and missing uncertainty
A plug-in approach substitutes \(\hat\theta\), often the posterior mean, and uses \(\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\hat\theta)\). With \(\hat\theta=\mu\), its variance is \(m\mu(1-\mu)\), omitting \[m(m-1)\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid y).\] Indeed, the law of total variance gives \[\operatorname{Var}(K\mid y)=E[m\theta(1-\theta)\mid y]+\operatorname{Var}(m\theta\mid y).\] For \(m>1\) and positive posterior variance the full predictive count distribution is more dispersed. For a single future Bernoulli trial (\(m=1\)), mixing yields Bernoulli probability \(\mu\), so this particular plug-in predictive distribution is exact.

mu <- A/(A+B)
c(full_variance = m*mu*(1-mu)*(A+B+m)/(A+B+1),
  plugin_variance = m*mu*(1-mu))

  full_variance plugin_variance 
      10.408163        4.591837 


Future trials are independent conditional on \(\theta\), but positively associated after integrating out their common uncertain parameter.

title: Unit 6: Predictive Distributions
text:
Prior predictive checks
Before observing these data, \[f(y_{\rm new})=\int f(y_{\rm new}\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta.\] For a \(\operatorname{Beta}(a,b)\) prior and a future binomial count, this is the same beta-binomial formula with \(a,b\) replacing \(A,B\). Simulate plausible data under the sampling design and ask whether their range, extreme values, and frequencies agree with domain knowledge. Revise implausible priors before using the same observations to update them.

set.seed(254)
a <- 2; b <- 2; m <- 20
prior_theta <- rbeta(50000, a, b)
prior_y <- rbinom(length(prior_theta), m, prior_theta)
hist(prior_y, breaks = seq(-0.5, m+0.5, by = 1), probability = TRUE,
     main = "Prior predictive check", xlab = "Successes in 20 trials")







c(prob_extreme = mean(prior_y == 0 | prior_y == m))

prob_extreme 
      0.0227 



Connection to the marginal likelihood
The marginal likelihood is the prior predictive mass/density evaluated at the observed data. For an observed count \(s\) from \(n\) trials, \[f(s)=\binom ns\frac{B(a+s,b+n-s)}{B(a,b)}.\] For a particular ordered Bernoulli sequence, the binomial coefficient is absent. The sample space must match what was observed. The posterior predictive uses the updated posterior; the marginal likelihood uses the prior. Proper priors are essential for well-defined prior predictive distributions and usual marginal-likelihood comparisons.

title: Unit 6: Predictive Distributions
text:
Check your understanding
Why should you not draw an independent posterior \(\theta\) for each future trial within one batch? That changes the assumed shared-rate model and removes the within-batch dependence induced by parameter uncertainty.

title: Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
text: Based on the corresponding unit in the supplied STAT 251 Midterm Exam Topics guide. Numerical examples are illustrative, not additional course data.

title: Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
text:
Bernoulli and binomial sampling
For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta)\), \(Y\in\{0,1\}\), \[P(Y=y\mid\theta)=\theta^y(1-\theta)^{1-y},\quad E(Y)=\theta,\quad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\theta(1-\theta).\] If \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are iid Bernoulli given \(\theta\), then \(S=\sum_iY_i\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\theta)\): \[P(S=s\mid\theta)=\binom ns\theta^s(1-\theta)^{n-s},\quad s=0,\ldots,n.\] Its mean is \(n\theta\) and variance is \(n\theta(1-\theta)\). The parameter \(\theta\) is the common success probability per trial, not the number of successes. The binomial assumptions require a fixed trial count, binary outcomes, and conditional independence with a common probability.

title: Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
section: Beta priors: support, moments, and shape
text:
Beta priors: support, moments, and shape
For \(a,b>0\), \[\pi(\theta)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}\mathbf1_{(0,1)}(\theta),\quad
B(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}.\] The density is positive on \((0,1)\) (its topological support is \([0,1]\)), with no point mass at either endpoint. \[E(\theta)=\frac a{a+b},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta)=\frac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}.\]
When \(a=b=1\) it is uniform. Both parameters above one give an interior mode \((a-1)/(a+b-2)\). Both below one give a U-shaped density; \(a<1\) gives a singularity near zero and \(b<1\) near one. With one shape at most one and the other at least one, it is monotone except for the uniform case. Equal shapes yield symmetry; \(a>b\) puts the mean above one-half.

title: Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
text:
Credible intervals and confidence intervals

a <- 2; b <- 2; s <- 7; n <- 10
A <- a+s; B <- b+n-s
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), A, B)

[1] 0.3857383 0.8614207


Conditional on the data, prior, and likelihood, this equal-tailed interval has posterior probability 0.95 of containing \(\theta\). A frequentist 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. Its coverage statement is about the procedure, not a posterior probability assigned to the realized interval.

title: Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
text:
Plot prior, likelihood, and posterior

t <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 1000)
prior <- dbeta(t, a, b)
post <- dbeta(t, A, B)
# Scale likelihood to integrate to one only for a common plotting scale.
scaled_lik <- dbeta(t, s+1, n-s+1)
matplot(t, cbind(prior, scaled_lik, post), type = "l", lty = c(2,3,1),
        col = c("gray40", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
        xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "Density / scaled likelihood")
legend("topleft", c("Prior", "Scaled likelihood", "Posterior"),
       col = c("gray40", "steelblue", "firebrick"), lty = c(2,3,1), bty = "n")








The likelihood favors values near \(s/n\); the prior adjusts their relative weights. Scaling the likelihood for display does not make it a posterior under the chosen prior.

title: Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
text:
Bayesian hypothesis testing
For \(H_+:\theta>0.5\) versus \(H_-:\theta\leq0.5\), compute posterior region probabilities:

p_prior <- pbeta(0.5, a, b, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_post <- pbeta(0.5, A, B, lower.tail = FALSE)
c(posterior_Hplus = p_post,
  BF_plus_minus = (p_post/(1-p_post))/(p_prior/(1-p_prior)))

posterior_Hplus   BF_plus_minus 
      0.8665771       6.4949680 


Posterior odds equal prior odds times the Bayes factor for these complementary hypotheses with the prior’s induced conditional distributions. These are not p-values. A continuous beta prior gives \(P(\theta=0.5)=0\) before and after updating. Testing an exact point null against an alternative with positive posterior null probability requires an explicit prior point mass and model probabilities. A decision also depends on the losses of incorrect actions.

title: Unit 4: Beta-Binomial Inference
text:
Prior elicitation

Objective priors
Common defaults include the uniform \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) and Jeffreys \(\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,1/2)\) prior. They encode different information; uniformity depends on parameterization. The formal Haldane kernel corresponds to \(a=b=0\) and is improper; its posterior is proper only if both successes and failures occur. Prefer a proper prior for predictive calculations and marginal likelihoods.


Data augmentation: prior successes and failures
Starting with \(\operatorname{Beta}(a_0,b_0)\), adding hypothetical \(s_0\) successes and \(f_0\) failures gives \(\operatorname{Beta}(a_0+s_0,b_0+f_0)\). Relative to a uniform baseline, the added counts are \(a-1,b-1\), when nonnegative. The common shorthand of calling \(a,b\) prior counts describes the update algebra; always state the baseline convention. Hypothetical observations are an elicitation device, not actual new data.


Method of moments
Given a desired mean \(\mu\) and variance \(v\), set \[\kappa=\frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{v}-1,\quad a=\mu\kappa,\quad b=(1-\mu)\kappa,\] requiring \(0<\mu<1\) and \(0<v<\mu(1-\mu)\).

mu <- 0.6; v <- 0.02
kappa <- mu*(1-mu)/v - 1
c(a = mu*kappa, b = (1-mu)*kappa)

  a   b 
6.6 4.4 




Prior strength versus sample size
For \(n>0\), the posterior mean is \[\frac{a+s}{a+b+n}=\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\frac a{a+b}
+\frac n{a+b+n}\frac sn.\] The concentration \(a+b\) acts as a prior effective sample size in this mean-weighting sense. A large concentration relative to \(n\) pulls the result toward the prior mean; large \(n\) gives the sample proportion more weight. Compare plausible priors to assess sensitivity, especially with small samples.

title: Unit 2: Probability and R Foundations
section: Conditional probability, total probability, and Bayes’ rule
text:
Conditional probability, total probability, and Bayes’ rule
For \(P(B)>0\), \[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.\] For a mutually exclusive, exhaustive partition \(H_1,\ldots,H_k\), \[P(B)=\sum_jP(B\mid H_j)P(H_j),\qquad
P(H_i\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid H_i)P(H_i)}{\sum_jP(B\mid H_j)P(H_j)}.\] Identify the hypotheses, assign prior probabilities, compute the evidence under each, and normalize. Do not interchange \(P(B\mid H)\) and \(P(H\mid B)\).

Worked application
A machine is from supplier A with probability 0.3 and B with probability 0.7. Defect rates are 0.08 and 0.02. Given a defect \(D\), \[P(A\mid D)=\frac{0.08(0.3)}{0.08(0.3)+0.02(0.7)}\approx0.632.\]

prior <- c(A = 0.3, B = 0.7)
likelihood <- c(A = 0.08, B = 0.02)
evidence <- sum(prior * likelihood)
prior * likelihood / evidence

        A         B 
0.6315789 0.3684211

title: Unit 2: Probability and R Foundations
text:
Random variables, support, and indicators

Discrete: probability mass functions
A pmf \(p(y)=P(Y=y)\) satisfies \(p(y)\geq0\) and \(\sum_y p(y)=1\). The support is the set of possible outcomes with positive mass. For a binomial variable it is \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) when \(0<\theta<1\).


Continuous: probability density functions
A pdf satisfies \(f(y)\geq0\) and \(\int f(y)\,dy=1\). Probabilities are areas: \[P(a<Y<b)=\int_a^b f(y)\,dy.\] For a continuous variable \(P(Y=y)=0\); density height is not probability and can exceed one. An indicator makes support explicit. For example, \[f(y)=\frac1{v-u}\mathbf1_{(u,v)}(y),\quad u<v.\] The indicator equals one on its specified set and zero elsewhere.


Cumulative distribution functions
For either type, \(F(t)=P(Y\leq t)\). It is nondecreasing, right-continuous, and approaches zero and one at the two tails. A discrete cdf has jumps. In general, \[P(a<Y\leq b)=F(b)-F(a).\] For discrete variables, inclusion or exclusion of endpoints can change the answer.

title: Unit 2: Probability and R Foundations
text:
Expectation and variance
\[E[g(Y)]=\sum_y g(y)p(y)\quad\text{or}\quad\int g(y)f(y)\,dy,\] when the expectation exists. With \(\mu=E(Y)\), \[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=E[(Y-\mu)^2]=E(Y^2)-\mu^2.\] Also \(E(a+bY)=a+bE(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(a+bY)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)\). Expectations add even without independence; variances add without covariance terms only when the covariances vanish.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Unit 1: Write a likelihood
Five iid Bernoulli observations contain four successes. Write the ordered-data likelihood and the count likelihood. Where is each maximized?






NoteSolution





Ordered-data likelihood: \(\theta^4(1-\theta)\). Count likelihood: \(5\theta^4(1-\theta)\). Both are maximized at \(4/5\). The count likelihood aggregates the five possible orders.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Unit 2: Invert a conditional probability
\(P(H)=0.2\), \(P(E\mid H)=0.8\), \(P(E\mid H^c)=0.1\). Find \(P(H\mid E)\).






NoteSolution





\(P(E)=0.8(0.2)+0.1(0.8)=0.24\), so \(P(H\mid E)=0.16/0.24=2/3\).

title: Practice Problems
text:
Unit 3: Interpret an interval
A posterior assigns probability 0.95 to \((0.3,0.7)\). What does this mean? Is it a statement about repeated-sample coverage?






NoteSolution





Given the observed data and assumed prior/model, the parameter lies in that interval with posterior probability 0.95. Repeated-sample coverage is a different property; it is not implied by this posterior statement alone.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Unit 4: Update and test
A Beta(2,3) prior is updated by eight successes in ten trials. Find the posterior mean, equal-tailed 95% interval, and posterior probability that \(\theta>0.5\).






NoteSolution





The posterior is Beta(10,5); its mean is \(10/15\).

c(mean = 10/15, probability = pbeta(0.5, 10, 5, lower.tail = FALSE))

       mean probability 
  0.6666667   0.9102173 

qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), 10, 5)

title: Practice Problems
text:
Unit 5: Monte Carlo precision
With 10,000 independent draws, a posterior probability estimate is 0.6. Estimate its MCSE. How many draws approximately halve it?






NoteSolution





\(\sqrt{0.6(0.4)/10000}\approx0.00490\). About 40,000 independent draws halve this MCSE. This calculation concerns computation, not posterior concentration.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Unit 6: Predict a count
With a Beta(10,5) posterior and five future trials, find the mean and variance of the future count. Compare with plug-in prediction.






NoteSolution





The mean is \(5(2/3)=10/3\). Full variance is \(5(2/3)(1/3)(20/16)=25/18\); plug-in variance is \(10/9\). The difference is \(5(4)\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid y)=5/18\).

title: Unit 1: Models and Likelihood
text:
Statistical models and model formulation
A statistical model is a family of probability distributions \[\mathcal M=\{f(y\mid\theta):\theta\in\Theta\}.\] Here \(y\) denotes possible data, \(\theta\) an unknown parameter, and \(\Theta\) the parameter space. A model represents assumptions about how observations arise; it is an approximation, not the data themselves.

Steps to formulate a model

Define the observational unit, outcome, sampling design, and scientific question.
Specify the outcome’s possible values (support) and choose a distribution compatible with them.
Define the unknown parameters and their allowed values.
State dependence and sampling assumptions, then write the joint distribution.
Use observations to estimate parameters or update uncertainty; check the model against the observed context and data.

For repeated binary outcomes, let \(Y_i=1\) denote success and \(Y_i=0\) failure. A Bernoulli model has \(\theta\in[0,1]\) and \[f(y_i\mid\theta)=\theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i}\mathbf1_{\{0,1\}}(y_i).\]


Independent and identically distributed observations
Conditional on a fixed \(\theta\), independence gives a product and identical distributions give the same factor form: \[f(\mathbf y\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i\mid\theta).\] For Bernoulli observations with \(s=\sum_i y_i\), \[f(\mathbf y\mid\theta)=\theta^s(1-\theta)^{n-s}.\] If only the count \(S=s\) is observed, its binomial pmf includes \(\binom ns\). That factor counts the possible sequences. It does not affect likelihood ratios in \(\theta\), but matters for probabilities of counts.

title: Unit 1: Models and Likelihood
text:
Data and the likelihood function
Before observing data, \(f(y\mid\theta)\) is a pmf/pdf in \(y\), with \(\theta\) fixed. After observing \(y_{\rm obs}\), \[L(\theta;y_{\rm obs})=f(y_{\rm obs}\mid\theta)\] is a function of \(\theta\), with data fixed. It measures relative compatibility with the observations. It is not a probability distribution for \(\theta\) and need not integrate to one over \(\Theta\).
Data enter fitting through this likelihood. In Bayesian inference they update a prior; they do not select a unique model without assumptions. Design flaws or dependence cannot be repaired merely by increasing sample size.

Executable likelihood example

y <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1)

n <- length(y)
s <- sum(y)

curve(dbinom(s, n, x),
      from = 0, to = 1,
      xlab = expression(theta),
      ylab = "Likelihood")

abline(v = s/n, lty = 2)








Subtracting the largest log likelihood prevents numerical underflow and rescales the maximum to one. The Bernoulli maximum likelihood estimate is \(\hat\theta=s/n\).

title: Unit 1: Models and Likelihood
text:
Check your understanding
Why can a factor independent of \(\theta\) be omitted when plotting relative likelihoods? Because it cancels in every likelihood ratio. Why can the iid product fail? Repeated measurements on the same person, for example, may remain dependent given the proposed parameter.

title: Unit 3: Bayesian Updating and Summaries
text:
Interpretations of probability
Symmetry (classical): equally plausible outcomes receive equal probabilities, as with an ideal fair die. Frequency: probability describes a limiting relative frequency in repeated trials under stable conditions. Subjective (Bayesian): probability represents a coherent degree of belief given information. Bayesian inference uses probability to describe uncertainty about unknown parameters as well as future data. Subjective does not mean arbitrary: beliefs should be justified and assessed for sensitivity.

title: Unit 3: Bayesian Updating and Summaries
text:
Bayes’ theorem for statistical models
For a continuous parameter and a proper prior, \[\pi(\theta\mid y_{\rm obs})=
\frac{f(y_{\rm obs}\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)}{f(y_{\rm obs})},\qquad
f(y_{\rm obs})=\int_\Theta f(y_{\rm obs}\mid t)\pi(t)\,dt.\] For a discrete parameter, replace the integral by a sum. The denominator must be positive and finite.

Four components







Component
Interpretation




Likelihood \(f(y_{\rm obs}\mid\theta)\)
How compatible each parameter is with the observed data


Prior \(\pi(\theta)\)
Uncertainty about the parameter before these data


Marginal likelihood \(f(y_{\rm obs})\)
Probability mass or density of these data averaged over the prior


Posterior \(\pi(\theta\mid y_{\rm obs})\)
Updated uncertainty about the parameter



The marginal likelihood is constant with respect to \(\theta\), since the parameter has been integrated out. It can vary with the data or the model. Therefore, \[\pi(\theta\mid y_{\rm obs})\propto L(\theta;y_{\rm obs})\pi(\theta).\] Proportionality identifies a kernel; a density still needs normalization. For continuous data the marginal likelihood is a density, not the probability of the exact observed point.

title: Unit 3: Bayesian Updating and Summaries
text:
Summarizing a posterior

Center and spread
The posterior mean is \(E(\theta\mid y)\); the median splits posterior mass equally; a mode maximizes posterior density (the MAP estimate). They need not coincide. The posterior standard deviation is \[\sqrt{E(\theta^2\mid y)-E(\theta\mid y)^2}.\] It measures remaining parameter uncertainty, not Monte Carlo error.


Region probabilities and credible intervals
\[P(\theta\in A\mid y)=\int_A\pi(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta.\] A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) credible interval contains posterior probability \(1-\alpha\). An equal-tailed interval uses quantiles \(\alpha/2\) and \(1-\alpha/2\). Highest posterior density regions instead collect high-density values; these summaries can differ for skewed or multimodal posteriors.

# Illustrative posterior Beta(9, 5)
A <- 9; B <- 5
c(mean = A/(A+B), median = qbeta(0.5, A, B),
  mode = (A-1)/(A+B-2), sd = sqrt(A*B/((A+B)^2*(A+B+1))))

     mean    median      mode        sd 
0.6428571 0.6498366 0.6666667 0.1237179 

qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), A, B)

[1] 0.3857383 0.8614207

pbeta(0.8, A, B) - pbeta(0.5, A, B)

[1] 0.7674465


The mode formula above requires both shape parameters to exceed one. Interpret the interval as a 95% posterior probability statement conditional on the observed data and assumed model/prior.

title: Unit 3: Bayesian Updating and Summaries
text:
Check your understanding
Does doubling a likelihood everywhere change the normalized posterior? No: the same factor multiplies its normalizing constant. Does a narrow posterior guarantee a good model? No: precision is conditional on the assumptions.

title: Unit 5: Monte Carlo Inference
text: Based on the corresponding unit in the supplied STAT 251 Midterm Exam Topics guide. Numerical examples are illustrative, not additional course data.

title: Unit 5: Monte Carlo Inference
text:
Monte Carlo expectations
If \(\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(J)}\) are iid draws from a posterior and \(E(|g(\theta)|\mid y)<\infty\), then \[E[g(\theta)\mid y]\approx\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^Jg(\theta^{(j)}).\] This is integration by simulation, justified by the law of large numbers. For nonlinear \(g\), \(E[g(\theta)]\) generally differs from \(g(E[\theta])\).

title: Unit 5: Monte Carlo Inference
text:
Means, variances, probabilities, and quantiles

set.seed(251)
J <- 50000
A <- 9; B <- 5
draws <- rbeta(J, A, B)
c(mean = mean(draws), variance = var(draws),
  mean_square = mean(draws^2), prob_region = mean(draws > 0.5 & draws < 0.8))

       mean    variance mean_square prob_region 
 0.64280644  0.01536732  0.42856713  0.76714000 

quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))

     2.5%       50%     97.5% 
0.3859137 0.6500028 0.8616998 

# Exact benchmarks for this conjugate example
c(mean = A/(A+B), variance = A*B/((A+B)^2*(A+B+1)),
  mean_square = A*(A+1)/((A+B)*(A+B+1)),
  prob_region = pbeta(0.8, A, B)-pbeta(0.5, A, B))

       mean    variance mean_square prob_region 
 0.64285714  0.01530612  0.42857143  0.76744654 

qbeta(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), A, B)

[1] 0.3857383 0.6498366 0.8614207


var uses denominator \(J-1\). A probability estimate is the mean of an indicator; empirical quantiles give an approximate equal-tailed credible interval. Strict and non-strict inequalities are equivalent here because the posterior is continuous.

title: Unit 5: Monte Carlo Inference
section: Monte Carlo error and number of draws
text:
Monte Carlo error and number of draws
Repeated independent simulations give slightly different estimates. For iid draws with finite variance, \[\operatorname{MCSE}(\overline g)\approx\frac{s_g}{\sqrt J}.\] For a probability estimate \(\hat p\), this becomes \(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/J}\). Four times as many draws roughly halves this error; precision improves at rate \(J^{-1/2}\).

p_hat <- mean(draws > 0.5)
c(mean_mcse = sd(draws)/sqrt(J),
  probability = p_hat, probability_mcse = sqrt(p_hat*(1-p_hat)/J),
  posterior_sd = sd(draws))

       mean_mcse      probability probability_mcse     posterior_sd 
    0.0005543883     0.8662200000     0.0015223857     0.1239649981 


MCSE measures computational uncertainty; posterior SD measures uncertainty about \(\theta\) given the data. Increasing \(J\) reduces the former, not the latter. A seed makes results reproducible but does not remove simulation error. The simple MCSE formula assumes independent draws; autocorrelated MCMC requires effective sample size. Quantile MCSE has a different formula and is larger in sparse tails. A zero estimated rare-event probability does not establish that the true probability is zero.

title: Unit 5: Monte Carlo Inference
text:
Compare two proportions
Suppose independent groups have independent beta priors and conditionally independent binomial data. Then the joint posterior factorizes: \[\theta_1\mid y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a_1+s_1,b_1+n_1-s_1),\quad
\theta_2\mid y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a_2+s_2,b_2+n_2-s_2).\] Pair independent draws and calculate \(\Delta^{(j)}=\theta_1^{(j)}-\theta_2^{(j)}\).

set.seed(252)
J <- 50000
theta1 <- rbeta(J, 2+18, 2+30-18)
theta2 <- rbeta(J, 2+12, 2+28-12)
delta <- theta1-theta2
p <- mean(delta > 0)
c(prob_group1_higher = p, mcse = sqrt(p*(1-p)/J),
  mean_difference = mean(delta))

prob_group1_higher               mcse    mean_difference 
       0.892400000        0.001385801        0.150233454 

quantile(delta, c(0.025, 0.975))

       2.5%       97.5% 
-0.08719196  0.38041505 

hist(delta, breaks = 50, probability = TRUE,
     xlab = expression(theta[1]-theta[2]), main = "Posterior difference")
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)








The probability estimates evidence that group 1 has the larger underlying rate. The credible interval describes the size and uncertainty of the difference. Do not subtract marginal interval endpoints to obtain an interval for a difference. If the posterior parameters are dependent, draw jointly from their joint posterior instead of independently.
